summary: XRD analysis of CsPbBr3 nanocrystals (NC492 and NC517) annealed at various temperatures shows that the cubic perovskite phase is retained across all conditions, with no detectable phase transitions. Peak positions remain constant, while peak intensities increase and widths narrow slightly with higher annealing temperatures, suggesting improved crystallinity.

key_findings.finding: XRD peak positions for both NC492 and NC517 remain unchanged across all annealing temperatures (300 K to 400 K), matching standard cubic CsPbBr3.
Peak intensities increase and peak widths become slightly narrower with increasing annealing temperature for both samples.

scientific_interpretation.claim: The retention of identical peak positions across all temperatures and both samples indicates that the cubic perovskite phase of CsPbBr3 is stable under the annealing conditions studied.
scientific_interpretation.reasoning: All XRD patterns for NC492 and NC517 at different temperatures show the same set of peak positions, which match the standard cubic CsPbBr3 reference.

citations.evidence: The patterns of standard cubic CsPbBr 3 perovskite structure (JCPDS No. 54-0752) at room temperature are shown in the figure for comparison.

scientific_interpretation.claim: The increase in peak intensity and narrowing of peak widths with higher annealing temperature suggest improved crystallinity of CsPbBr3 nanocrystals.
scientific_interpretation.reasoning: The reported trends indicate that annealing enhances crystal quality, as evidenced by sharper and more intense XRD peaks.

citations.evidence: Peak intensities increase with annealing temperature; Peak widths become slightly narrower at higher temperatures

limitations.claim: No quantitative FWHM or lattice parameter data are provided, limiting the ability to precisely assess crystallite size or strain.
Phase identification relies on peak positions only; absence of secondary phases cannot be fully confirmed without more sensitive analysis or reporting of minor peaks.
No information is provided on possible changes in preferred orientation (texture) or quantitative phase fraction with annealing.

citations.evidence: No mention of texture or phase fraction analysis in fig_4.analysis
